Reading is crowded, and mostly open

19 items turn pages and recordings into text, and 16 of them are open: Kraken, eScriptorium, Qwen3-VL, dots.ocr, AnandaSky, Polyscriptor, Whisper. A scholar can run this stage without a commercial model.

Only 4 items, from Meelen and from Li, Zhong & McManus. The step from a diplomatic transcription to searchable standard text has the fewest tools, and in Meelen's published results hand-written rules beat her neural systems.
Analysis is the largest stage, and where commercial models sit

29 items: LLMs coding variables, scoring books, generating data and minting conjectures (Celli, Pink, Turchin, Stefanski). Commercial models are used mostly here and for annotation, rarely for reading.
Building is a layer of its own
19 items: coding agents, Claude skills, AGENTS.md files and prompt sets (Dows-Miller, Kiessling, Grant, Rabus). How scholars build and steer their tools was a topic in its own right.
20 items, and half have no public link: many talks validate against hand-built gold standards or human coding that are not published.
Only one project retrains a general LLM

Nehrdich's MITRA continues pretraining Qwen3.5 on about 30 billion tokens of Buddhist texts. Others train smaller task models (AnandaSky, Meelen's handwriting models, Polyscriptor) or use frontier models as they are.
